name: Kids in Need of Defense: advocacy and communications (charityevals' estimate)
summary: KIND's advocacy and communications ($4.2 million in 2024, about $3.6 million a year over 2023-2024 in 2024 prices) are counted as a past average over the period's wins: its share as one of five counsel in the J.O.P. v. DHS settlement (approved November 2024), which keeps thousands of former unaccompanied children's asylum claims with USCIS's asylum officers rather than immigration court, and the District of Columbia's 2024 Vulnerable Youth Guardianship Protection Amendment Act, each valued per status gained as in charityevals' model of KIND's legal services, plus a judged share for wins not modelled one by one. With its next dollar at 67% of the average, it comes to about 0.009 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, far below the site's global-health median because the two wins change the status of only a few hundred people a year and KIND's share of the J.O.P. counsel's resources is small (about a tenth). The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges alone spanning over ten thousandfold (the class size, the gain in the chance of asylum, KIND's share of counsel, the wins not modelled), and both wins are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Class members of J.O.P. v. DHS who apply for asylum with USCIS under the settlement
rows.explainer: The class is people determined to be unaccompanied children who applied for asylum after 31 May 2019, or did so by 24 February 2025, and whom a 2019 USCIS policy would have sent to an adversarial immigration court hearing because they had turned 18 or reunited with a parent. No count is published (Public Counsel's case page speaks of the policy 'threatening the safety of thousands of children who have filed for asylum'). Anchors: over half a million unaccompanied children were referred to federal custody in fiscal years 2019-2024 (ORR), most of them 15-17 and released to a parent or relative, so most turn 18 or are with a parent by the time they file; only a minority file for asylum at all (many pursue Special Immigrant Juvenile status instead), and USCIS's asylum offices take several thousand such filings a year. Our judgment 8,000 class members who benefit, from 2,000 to 30,000.

rows.label: Rise in a class member's chance of asylum from USCIS's initial jurisdiction
rows.explainer: The settlement keeps these cases with USCIS's asylum officers, in a non-adversarial interview built for children, instead of contested court hearings, lifts the one-year filing deadline for class members, and bars removal while USCIS decides. Anchors: TRAC's study of children's cases found 73% of represented children allowed to remain against 15% alone (most class members have counsel either way), and asylum offices grant children's claims more often than immigration courts, where government attorneys contest them; neither agency publishes grant rates for this class. Our judgment +10 percentage points, from 3 to 25.

rows.label: Share of the J.O.P. litigation's work done in 2023-2024
rows.explainer: The suit ran from 2019 (with an injunction that year); the settlement was negotiated and approved in 2024 and enforced since. The cost counted is 2023-2024's, so only that period's share of the win is credited: 40%, from 20% to 60%.

rows.label: J.O.P.: units of value a year of the period, before adjustments
rows.explainer: A one-time cohort's gain, the period's share of it, spread over the period's years.

rows.label: J.O.P.: share that would not have come without the suit
rows.explainer: A later administration might have withdrawn the 2019 policy on its own (the 2024 settlement came under one that did not), and some class members would have won asylum in court anyway (that is in the relief gain). Our judgment 60%, from 30% to 90%.

rows.label: Organisations and firms counsel for the J.O.P. class

source.title: Public Counsel, J.O.P. v. DHS (case page)
source.quote: Public Counsel, the National Immigration Project, Bet Tzedek Legal Services, Kids In Need of Defense (KIND), and Goodwin Procter LLP

rows.explainer: KIND is one of five counsel; Goodwin Procter, a large firm, gave most of the litigation hours pro bono.

rows.label: KIND's share of the counsel's resources, against an equal split
rows.explainer: A large firm's pro bono team (Goodwin Procter, whose address is the class counsel contact on the class notices) carries most of the litigation hours in cases like this; KIND and the other legal-aid groups supply class representatives, practice alerts and implementation work (KIND hosts the class notices and practice alerts on its site). Our judgment half of an equal fifth, from a quarter to 1.2 (KIND among the leads).

rows.label: J.O.P.: KIND's share of the resources behind the win
rows.explainer: About 10%.

rows.label: J.O.P.: share of the settlement applied in practice
rows.explainer: The government has not kept to the settlement in full: the court granted a motion to enforce in 2025 (barring removal of class members awaiting USCIS), found the government in civil contempt in July 2026 and extended the agreement to November 2026, and USCIS paused asylum decisions in 2025. Our judgment 70% of the settlement's benefit delivered, from 40% to 100%.

rows.label: J.O.P.: years until class members' asylum decisions
rows.explainer: Applications filed by February 2025 are decided over the following years, slowed by USCIS's asylum backlog and its 2025 pauses: 1.5 years, from 0.5 to 3.

rows.label: J.O.P.: the wait, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: J.O.P.: missing-data step
rows.explainer: The class size, the gain in the chance of relief and the value of status are our judgments: the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Young immigrants a year who petition under the D.C. act's guardianship
rows.explainer: The Vulnerable Youth Guardianship Protection Amendment Act (D.C. Law 25-188, effective 19 July 2024, D.C. Code §21-2381 ff., code.dccouncil.gov; KIND's report, p. 5: 'Successfully advocated for') sets up a guardianship for noncitizens aged 18 to 20 whose reunification with a parent is not viable because of abuse, abandonment or neglect, with findings that track the Special Immigrant Juvenile ones: the state-court step a SIJS petition needs after 18. D.C. is small: a few dozen to a few hundred such petitions a year. Our judgment 60, from 20 to 200.

rows.label: Rise in such a youth's chance of permanent status
rows.explainer: Many of these youths could already seek guardianship under D.C.'s earlier law; the act removes obstacles for some. Our judgment +30 percentage points, from 10 to 60.

rows.label: Years a won law counts

rows.label: Years until the D.C. act brings status
rows.explainer: In force from July 2024; a youth's guardianship order then leads to a Special Immigrant Juvenile approval about 1.5 years later (USCIS processing; 0.5 to 3), and the green card later still: 2 years in all, from 0.5 to 4.

rows.label: Wins not modelled one by one, as a share of the two above
rows.explainer: KIND's other policy work in the period: defending federal appropriations for unaccompanied children's legal representation (the programme behind most of the casework in the legal-services model; appropriations are hard to move: Baumgartner et al., Lobbying and Policy Change, 2009, find most advocacy campaigns change nothing), the Keeping Kids Safe campaign for a children's immigration court, Europe's protections for unaccompanied and Ukrainian children, and communications. Its biggest past win, the federal programme itself, came before the period, and the programme was cut off in 2025. Our judgment 30%, from 0 to 100%, as for IRAP's advocacy model (30%, from 0 to 100%).

rows.label: Backlash, as a share
rows.explainer: Litigation against the government and public campaigns on immigration can harden policy; KIND and other providers were targeted by federal investigators in 2025. -2%, from -10% to 0.

rows.label: Wellbeing of security from removal beyond consumption, as a share
rows.explainer: Consumption misses the relief of no longer fearing removal: when mothers became eligible for deferred action (DACA), their children's anxiety and adjustment disorder diagnoses fell by more than half (Hainmueller et al., Science 2017). 15%, from 0 to 40%, as in the legal-services model.

rows.label: Remittances to the families at home, as a share
rows.explainer: A young person who gains status and works in the US sends money home, where it raises a much poorer household's consumption (remittances are about a fifth of GDP in Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala); the model counts only the person's own consumption. 6%, from 0 (little is sent) to 20% (large, lasting remittances), as in the legal-services model.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share
rows.explainer: The sum of the three shares above.
